question: What is the main thing that happens in neoplasia?

options.B: Rapid healing of acute tissue damage
options.C: Temporary swelling caused by local infection
options.D: Normal replacement of dead skin cells

explanation: Think of neoplasia as new growth that just won't quit! The cells keep multiplying without listening to the body's normal stop signals. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why do cancer cells keep growing even after the original tissue injury is gone?

options.A: They receive constant growth signals from nearby nerves
options.B: Scar tissue forces them to keep dividing rapidly
options.C: The body actively pumps extra blood into the tumor
options.D: Their internal regulatory machinery is permanently damaged

explanation: You got this! Inside these cells, the internal control buttons are broken, so they keep multiplying on their own without needing an outside trigger. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which of these is a classic feature of a benign tumor?

options.A: It grows very fast and invades nearby muscle
options.B: It has poorly differentiated, weird-looking cells
options.C: It easily spreads through the lymphatic system
options.D: It stays localized inside a fibrous capsule

explanation: Benign is friendly! These tumors stay neatly wrapped up in their own little capsule and don't try to invade the surrounding tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h2)

question: What makes a malignant tumor much more dangerous than a benign one?

options.A: Their tendency to cause severe local pain within days of starting
options.B: The fact that they always grow much larger than benign lumps
options.C: The complete absence of blood vessels inside their tissue mass
options.D: The ability to invade nearby structures and spread to distant organs

explanation: Malignant cells are troublemakers because they don't stay put. They love to break away and travel to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h2)

question: What happens when a normal proto-oncogene gets mutated?

options.A: It turns into an oncogene that drives nonstop cell division
options.B: It immediately forces the cell to undergo programmed death
options.C: It repairs all surrounding damaged DNA strands instantly
options.D: It stops all cellular activity and puts the cell to sleep

explanation: Proto-oncogenes are like the gas pedal for cell growth. When mutated, they become oncogenes that push the pedal all the way down! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the normal job of a tumor suppressor gene in a healthy cell?

options.A: act as a brake on cell division and fix DNA errors
options.B: stimulate rapid tissue repair after a physical injury
options.C: transport waste products away from dividing cells
options.D: supply extra blood and oxygen to growing tissues

explanation: Think of tumor suppressor genes as the safety brakes. They slow down cell division and patch up any DNA mistakes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the very first thing that happens during the initiation phase of cancer development?

options.A: The immune system completely destroys the mutated cell
options.B: New blood vessels sprout to feed the growing tumor mass
options.C: Abnormal cells spread through blood to distant organs
options.D: Permanent damage or mutation happens to the cell DNA

explanation: Initiation is the starting spark—it's that first permanent hit or change to the cell's DNA caused by a carcinogen. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h4)

question: During which phase of cancer development do cells gain aggressive traits and learn to spread?
explanation: Progression is the final, full-speed-ahead phase where the cells become truly malignant and start invading. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h4)

question: What chemical signal do growing tumors release to tell new blood vessels to grow?
explanation: VEGF is the chemical helper tumors use to build their own private highway system of blood vessels (angiogenesis). [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why do growing malignant tumors desperately need angiogenesis?

options.A: It supplies necessary oxygen and nutrients while removing metabolic waste
options.B: It provides a hard outer shell that keeps the tumor tightly enclosed
options.C: It protects the tumor cells from being destroyed by radiation therapy
options.D: It prevents white blood cells from attacking the cancerous mass

explanation: Just like us, tumors need food and oxygen to keep growing, plus a way to take out the trash! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h5)

question: What special tools do cancer cells use to break through surrounding tissue barriers?
explanation: MMPs act like little scissors or chemical drills, helping cancer cells chew through the matrix and invade surrounding tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h6)

question: A patient has colon cancer, and a scan shows the cancer has now traveled to the liver. What is this secondary growth called?
explanation: When cancer cells pack their bags and travel from their original home to a brand new organ, we call it metastasis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the term for the severe muscle wasting and extreme weight loss seen in many advanced cancer patients?
explanation: Cancer cachexia is a tough syndrome where the body rapidly wastes away its muscle and fat, despite eating. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h7)

question: What causes paraneoplastic syndromes in cancer patients?

options.A: The cancer spreads directly into the spinal cord and blocks nerve signals
options.B: The patient develops a severe secondary bacterial infection
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs destroy the patient's bone marrow completely
options.D: The tumor releases hormones or proteins that affect distant body systems

explanation: Even though they are far away from the tumor, other organs act up because the tumor secretes confusing hormones and proteins into the blood. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h7)
